items.title: Researchers find a faster way to pair socks
items.author: Sam Example
items.body:
Researchers at a fictional university say they have found a faster way to pair socks after laundry day, using nothing more than a shallow tray and a little patience.

The method sorts socks by colour first and by length second, which the team claims cuts the average pairing time by more than half for households of four or more people.

"We expected a small improvement," one of the researchers said in a statement. "We did not expect people to start enjoying the process."

The study followed sixty volunteers over twelve weeks. Each household recorded how long it took to pair every load, and how many socks remained without a partner at the end.

Lonely socks were reduced as well, although the authors caution that their sample was small and that the washing machine itself remains the main suspect.

What comes next

The team now plans a larger trial with a partner laundromat, and hopes to publish an open dataset of sock colours later this year.

Critics point out that the tray method requires counter space that many small apartments simply do not have.

items.title: City lights will dim when nobody is around
items.author: Sam Example
items.body:
A city council somewhere has voted to replace its ageing street lights with models that dim automatically when nobody is around, a change it expects to save a third of the lighting budget.

The new lights use simple motion sensors and brighten within a second when a pedestrian or cyclist approaches. Residents in a pilot street reported that they barely noticed the difference.

Wildlife groups welcomed the decision, saying darker nights help insects and bats that are confused by constant artificial light.

The council will roll out the lights district by district over the next two years, starting with residential streets and leaving main roads fully lit for now.

items.title: Volunteers restore a 1970s pinball machine
items.author: Robin Example
items.body:
A small team of volunteers has finished restoring a 1970s pinball machine that had been sitting in a barn for decades, and is now touring it around local libraries.

Most parts could be cleaned and repaired, but the scoring reels had to be rebuilt from scratch using drawings found in an old service manual.

Visitors can play for free; donations go to a youth club that teaches basic electronics.
